title: Angular Velocity and Acceleration with Calculus
short: ω = dθ/dt and α = dω/dt; integrate α(t) to find ω and θ.
trouble: Students differentiate an angle given in degrees and treat the result as radians per second.

blocks.html: Rotational Kinematics handled spinning with constant angular acceleration. Everything you did in Velocity and Position from Acceleration carries over to rotation with one change of letters: $x \to \theta$, $v \to \omega$, $a \to \alpha$.

$$\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}, \qquad \alpha = \dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}, \qquad \omega(t) = \omega_0 + \int_0^t \alpha\,dt'.$$ Angles in radians, $\omega$ in rad/s, $\alpha$ in rad/s². Every point of a rigid body shares the same $\theta$, $\omega$ and $\alpha$.

A radian is defined as arc length divided by radius, $\theta = s/r$, so it is a pure number and $s = r\theta$ holds exactly. Differentiating gives $v = r\omega$ and $a_t = r\alpha$ for a point at distance $r$ from the axis. Those simple links, and the formulas for rotational energy and work built on them, only hold with angles measured in radians.

opts.task: Change $\omega$. Every marked point turns through the same angle; the outer points move faster.

blocks.cap: Points at different radii share one $\theta$ and one $\omega$, but their speeds $v = r\omega$ differ.

blocks.title: Differentiate the angle
blocks.q: A turntable's angle is $\theta(t) = 2t^3 - 3t^2$ (rad, s). Find $\omega$ and $\alpha$ at $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

blocks.title: Integrate the angular acceleration
blocks.q: A wheel spinning at $3\ \text{rad/s}$ has $\alpha(t) = 4 - 2t$ (rad/s², s). Find $\omega$ and the angle turned at $t = 3\ \text{s}$.

blocks.html: Differentiating an angle given in degrees and calling the result rad/s. If $\theta = 30t^2$ degrees, then at $t = 2\ \text{s}$, $d\theta/dt = 120$ degrees per second, which is $120 \times \pi/180 = 2.09\ \text{rad/s}$, not 120 rad/s. Check: before using $v = r\omega$, $K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ or $P = \tau\omega$, make sure the angle was in radians; multiply degrees by $\pi/180$ and revolutions by $2\pi$.

head: Straight line
Rotation
Link for a point at radius $r$
rows: $a_t = r\alpha$, and also $a_c = r\omega^2$ toward the axis
blocks.cap: Every kinematics method has a rotational twin.

blocks.html: Angular velocity is really a vector, $\vec{\omega}$, pointing along the axis: curl the fingers of your right hand the way the object turns, and your thumb points along $\vec{\omega}$. In fixed-axis problems we keep just its sign, but the vector form is what makes Torque as a Cross Product and Gyroscopes and Precession work.
Revolutions per minute (rpm) are common on motors: $1\ \text{rpm} = \dfrac{2\pi}{60}\ \text{rad/s} \approx 0.105\ \text{rad/s}$.
